in special relativity, the speed of light (c) is the ultimate speed limit because of the way space and time are interwoven. einstein's theory shows that as an object moves faster, its relativistic mass increases, and the energy required to accelerate it approaches infinity as it nears c. this is described by the lorentz factor (γ = 1/√(1 - v²/c²)), which diverges to infinity as v approaches c. thus, accelerating an object beyond c would require infinite energy, which is impossible.  

additionally, exceeding c would violate causality—events could be observed in reverse order in different reference frames, breaking the logical sequence of cause and effect. the invariance of the speed of light in all inertial frames ensures that no information or matter can travel faster than light, preserving the consistency of physical laws across observers.
